name: Jaw clenching

lead: Jaw clenching means contracting the jaw-closing muscles, mainly the masseter and temporalis, by pressing the teeth together. In looksmaxxing it is promoted as a free alternative to chewing gum for growing the masseters, which can add width and definition to the lower face.

In dentistry the same behaviour, when habitual, is called bruxism. Clinicians note that people who clench or grind can develop enlarged masseters, and that this can be visible from outside; they also document tooth wear, jaw pain and headaches in some people. Looksmax.org threads disagree on whether clenching changes the jawline at all.

paras: Looksmaxxers describe deliberate, usually light, clenching sessions, sometimes with a cloth or soft material between the teeth, as a substitute for hard gum chewing. Results are described as gradual muscle-driven changes in the lower face.

Bruxism is associated with tooth wear and fractures, masticatory muscle pain, temporomandibular joint pain and headaches. Dental consensus statements describe it as a behaviour that can be a risk factor for such problems, and dentists often manage it with splints, behavioural measures or botulinum toxin.

chain: Repeated clenching loads the masseter and temporalis
angle.text: People who clench deliberately aim for masseter growth as a jaw-training alternative to gum chewing, seeking a fuller lower face. Clinicians report that habitual clenchers can develop visibly larger masseters.

lead: Jaw clenching is the sustained or repeated tightening of the jaw-closing muscles with the teeth together. Dentistry groups it with grinding under the term bruxism, defined by an international expert consensus as repetitive jaw-muscle activity characterised by clenching or grinding of the teeth and/or bracing or thrusting of the mandible, occurring during sleep or wakefulness.[1][2]

In looksmaxxing, clenching is discussed as a way to train the masseter, the thick cheek-side muscle that closes the jaw. Wikipedia notes that habitual clenching or grinding can enlarge the masseter, and that the enlargement is visible outside the mouth and can change facial appearance.[3][4] Posters on looksmax.org compare it with mewing and with chewing, with views ranging from "clenching is pure cope" to claims that it is a superior skull-remodelling habit.[5][6][7]
Clinical research focuses on bruxism as a condition: its causes, consequences and treatments, including occlusal splints and botulinum toxin to reduce masseter thickness.[8][9]

paras: The 2013 consensus definition treats bruxism as muscle activity that can be awake or sleep related; a 2018 update concluded that in otherwise healthy people it should be regarded as a behaviour that can be a risk, or protective, factor for certain clinical consequences rather than a disorder in itself.[1][2] Awake bruxism usually involves semivoluntary clenching and is often linked to stress or concentration, while sleep bruxism is centrally regulated and tied to sleep arousals.[3]

Bite force during clenching is far higher than the force of the tongue or gravity, a comparison that clenching advocates make on looksmax.org when contrasting it with mewing.[6] Studies in dental research have examined how clenching intensity changes bite force balance and occlusal contact.[10]

Masseter hypertrophy is a recognised sign of bruxism: the enlarged muscle is soft, usually bilateral, and visible outside the mouth, and uneven enlargement can cause facial asymmetry; people sometimes seek care after comments about their face.[3][4] A clinical overview notes that bruxism may lead to masticatory muscle hypertrophy as well as tooth surface loss and fractures.[11]
Within looksmaxxing, believers describe the enlargement as a jaw-widening, jawline-enhancing effect. Posters who disagree report never seeing clenching improve a jawline or create hollow cheeks.[5]

Reviews list headaches, temporomandibular joint pain, masticatory muscle pain, tooth wear, cracked teeth and prosthodontic complications among the consequences of bruxism, while noting that many people have no symptoms.[3][12] A systematic review examined the relationship between bruxism and temporomandibular disorders.[13]

Management options described in clinical overviews include occlusal splints, biofeedback, relaxation and sleep hygiene, and botulinum toxin; irreversible bite adjustments are described as lacking an evidence base.[11] A 2025 randomized comparison studied occlusal splint versus botulinum toxin for masseter thickness in people with bruxism.[9]

Threads include a "slight teeth grinding/clenching is superior to chewing" post that lists claimed advantages over gum such as no ghrelin-driven hunger, no laxative effect, less joint load and whole-skull remodelling, plus a suggestion to use a cloth rather than a mouth guard.[7] Others ask how to stop clenching in sleep or what bruxism is and how to fix it.[14][15]

Human research addresses bruxism rather than deliberate clenching for aesthetics. Consensus statements define the behaviour and grade its assessment.[1][2] A randomized trial of 16 healthy adults tested one month of gum-chewing training on masseter oxygen dynamics, muscle endurance and fatigue.[16] A randomized comparative trial examined occlusal splint versus botulinum toxin A on masseter thickness in bruxism.[9] Reviews cover treatments and risk factors, and note insufficient data to support a single standardised approach.[12][17]
